package_info.package_manager: Custom Windows malware (not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.why_malicious: ValleyRAT is a sophisticated multi-stage remote access trojan (RAT) targeting Windows systems. It employs in-memory shellcode execution, registry-based persistence, anti-analysis and AV evasion techniques, privilege escalation, and C2 communication to achieve full system compromise, user surveillance, and delivery of additional malicious payloads.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Creates mutex 'TEST'; deletes registry keys HKCU\Software\Console\IpDate and HKCU\Software\Console\IpDateInfo; stores C2 IP/port in HKCU\Software\Console\IpDateInfo = '|i:154.82.85.12|p:5689|'
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At initial execution, the code creates a mutex to enforce single instance, deletes previous persistence registry keys, and writes C2 configuration (IP and port) into the registry, enabling future C2 communication.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Manipulating registry keys to store C2 configuration and deleting prior persistence artifacts are common malware tactics to maintain control and evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not store C2 addresses in user registry keys or delete unrelated registry entries for persistence management.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may use mutexes for single-instance enforcement, but not for C2 configuration or registry key deletion.
key_indicators: Deletion of prior persistence registry keys

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Enumerates services for VM-related strings (e.g., 'VMWARE Tools', 'VirtualBox Guest'); terminates if found.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At startup, the code enumerates running services for virtualization-related strings and terminates execution if a virtual machine environment is detected, evading automated analysis.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: VM detection and conditional termination are established anti-analysis techniques used by malware to avoid detection in sandboxed or research environments.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely checks for VM artifacts or terminates based on their presence.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some licensing or DRM software may check for VMs, but typically does not terminate without user notification.
key_indicators: Service name checks for VM artifacts
Conditional process termination on VM detection

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Decodes shellcode with XOR 0x60; uses sleep obfuscation: modifies memory permissions, encodes/decodes shellcode, restores Sleep API, executes shellcode as callback for EnumSystemLocalesA.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During in-memory stage transition, the code decodes shellcode using XOR, modifies memory permissions to allow execution, obfuscates execution flow with Sleep API manipulation, and executes the shellcode as a callback, resulting in stealthy loading of the next-stage payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Memory permission changes, shellcode decoding, and callback-based execution are hallmarks of advanced malware seeking to evade static and dynamic analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not execute self-modifying shellcode or hijack API callbacks for code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some security or debugging tools may manipulate memory permissions, but not for self-modifying shellcode execution.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Sets HKCU\Software\Classes\mscfile\Shell\Open\Command to loader path; creates scheduled task for loader; abuses eventvwr.msc/CompMgmtLauncher.exe for auto-elevation.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During persistence setup, the code hijacks the mscfile registry handler to point to the loader, creates a scheduled task for automatic execution, and abuses Windows auto-elevate mechanisms to ensure the loader runs with high privileges at user login.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Registry hijacking and auto-elevation abuse are well-known persistence and privilege escalation techniques in malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not hijack mscfile handlers or create scheduled tasks for persistence without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise software may create scheduled tasks, but not by hijacking system handlers or abusing auto-elevation.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Invoke-Command -Command {Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath C:\}; kills AV processes; modifies registry keys to disable AV autostart.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During AV evasion, the code executes PowerShell commands to add Defender exclusions, terminates AV processes, and modifies registry keys to disable AV autostart, reducing the likelihood of detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Disabling AV, killing security processes, and modifying AV settings are direct indicators of malicious intent to evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not disable or interfere with security products.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administrators may use similar PowerShell commands for troubleshooting, but not in the context of malware deployment.
key_indicators: Registry modification of AV autostart settings

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Abuses ICMLuaUtil::ShellExec and fodhelper.exe with registry hijack (HKCU\Software\Classes\.pwn\Shell\Open\command, HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\CurVer) to launch malware with elevated privileges.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During privilege escalation, the code exploits Windows auto-elevate mechanisms by hijacking registry keys and abusing ICMLuaUtil::ShellExec and fodhelper.exe to launch the malware with administrator privileges without triggering a UAC prompt.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Abusing COM interfaces and system tools for silent privilege escalation is a recognized malware tactic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not hijack system handlers or registry keys to bypass UAC for elevation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate installers may use auto-elevate mechanisms, but not via registry hijacking or COM abuse.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Sends plaintext requests to C2 (e.g., GetRemoteShellcodeSize_{xor key}); receives XOR-encoded shellcode; injects into colorcpl.exe/cleanmgr.exe.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During C2 communication, the code sends plaintext requests to the C2 server, receives XOR-encoded shellcode, decodes it, and injects the payload into legitimate Windows processes for execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Network-based payload delivery, XOR encoding, and process injection are core RAT behaviors designed to evade detection and maintain persistence.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not fetch and inject shellcode from remote servers into system processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some update mechanisms may download code, but not as shellcode or via process injection.
key_indicators: Plaintext C2 requests with XOR-encoded responses

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Sends '64' or '32' to C2; receives XOR-encoded payload downloader; reflectively loads DLL; requests final ValleyRAT payload; stores shellcode in registry value d33f351a4aeea5e608853d1a56661059 on HKCU\Console\1.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During payload delivery, the code communicates with the C2 server to request architecture-specific payloads, receives and decodes a payload downloader, reflectively loads the ValleyRAT DLL, and stores shellcode in a registry value for stealthy execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Storing and executing shellcode from the registry and using reflective DLL loading are advanced techniques for stealth and evasion.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not store executable code in registry values or perform reflective DLL loading from C2-delivered payloads.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some security tools may use reflective DLL loading, but not in conjunction with registry-stored shellcode.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Supports commands: load plugin, write/execute file, download/execute from URL, send screenshots, clear event logs, update registry, enumerate processes, logoff/reboot/shutdown, create C2 session, prevent sleep, etc.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enables full remote control by supporting commands for plugin loading, file operations, downloading and executing files from URLs, screen capture, event log clearing, registry updates, process enumeration, system control, and maintaining C2 sessions, resulting in comprehensive victim monitoring and control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remote control, surveillance, and anti-forensics capabilities are core features of RATs and are not present in legitimate software.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not provide arbitrary remote command execution, screen capture, or event log clearing without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools may have some similar features, but are used with user knowledge and consent.

attack_chain.action: User executes malicious loader disguised as a financial document.
Loader obfuscates and executes in-memory shellcode to load next stage.
Beaconing module sets up persistence, disables AV, and escalates privileges.
Malware communicates with C2, downloads and injects next-stage payloads.
Payload downloader retrieves and loads ValleyRAT DLL, storing shellcode in registry.
ValleyRAT provides remote control, surveillance, and anti-forensics capabilities.

behavioral_signatures: In-memory shellcode execution with memory permission changes and callback hijacking
Registry-based persistence and C2 configuration under HKCU\Software\Console and HKCU\Software\Classes
Disabling or killing AV processes and modifying AV-related registry keys
Abuse of Windows auto-elevate mechanisms (eventvwr.msc, fodhelper.exe, ICMLuaUtil::ShellExec) for privilege escalation
Process injection into legitimate Windows binaries (colorcpl.exe, cleanmgr.exe)
Registry-stored shellcode (e.g., HKCU\Console\1\d33f351a4aeea5e608853d1a56661059) and reflective DLL loading
Remote command execution, screen capture, and event log clearing via RAT commands
file_indicators: Executables with Chinese financial document names (e.g., 工商年报大师.exe)
network_indicators: Plaintext C2 requests with XOR-encoded responses (e.g., GetRemoteShellcodeSize_{xor key})
Connections to http://www.baidu.com for connectivity check
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for suspicious registry modifications, especially under HKCU\Software\Console and HKCU\Software\Classes, and for the presence of shellcode in registry values. Detect in-memory shellcode execution with memory permission changes and callback hijacking. Watch for process injection into system binaries such as colorcpl.exe and cleanmgr.exe. Alert on AV process termination, PowerShell-based AV exclusions, and registry changes disabling AV autostart. Monitor network traffic for connections to known C2 IPs, plaintext C2 requests, and XOR-encoded responses. Flag creation of scheduled tasks or registry hijacks for persistence, and detect behaviors such as event log clearing, screen capture, and remote command execution indicative of RAT activity.
